summary: A collection of technical clarifications and implementation notes for DNSSEC, gathering errata that existed at the time. It updates RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035 and the NSEC3 specification, RFC 5155, and it also covers how NSEC3 and SHA-2 are used.

eli5.summary: A teacher hands out a page of fixes and hints for a tricky rulebook so everyone who builds the game plays it the same way.

subtitle: Errata and implementation advice for DNSSEC, sorted from security-critical fixes down to small corrections.

tldr.problem: The core DNSSEC documents (RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035) and the NSEC3 specification (RFC 5155) contained ambiguities, omissions and errors that could lead to security failures or interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: This document lists clarifications and corrections in order of importance: security-relevant validation rules first, then interoperability points, then minor fixes. It also makes NSEC3 and SHA-2 part of the core DNSSEC specification.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035 and RFC 5155, and has itself been updated by RFC 8749.

facts.label: CD bit on upstream queries
facts.value: SHOULD be set on every one

today: RFC 6840 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8749. It updates RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035 and RFC 5155, so implementors read it alongside those documents.

sections.title: What This Document Collects
sections.content:
This document lists additions, clarifications and corrections to the core DNSSEC specification in RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035, as later amended by RFC 5155. It serves implementors as a resource, and also as a list of known items that needed to be addressed when advancing the DNSSEC documents along the Standards Track.

The items are sorted by importance. The first ones are those that could lead to security problems if ignored, and the last are expected to have little operational impact.
sections.eli5: It is a checklist of fixes for a rulebook, with the most important fixes at the top.

sections.title: NSEC3, SHA-2 and the BAD Cache
sections.content:
Two sets of documents are declared part of core DNSSEC. RFC 5155 defines NSEC3 and NSEC3PARAM for hashed denial of existence. Validators are strongly encouraged to support it because a number of highly visible zones use it. The algorithm identifiers from RFC 5155 and RFC 5702 (RSASHA256 and RSASHA512) only signal that a zone might use NSEC3, so validators supporting them MUST support both NSEC3 and NSEC responses.

SHA-256 in DS records (RFC 4509) and the RSASHA256 and RSASHA512 algorithms (RFC 5702) are likewise now core, and validators are strongly encouraged to support them.

On scaling, the earlier permission for resolvers to keep a BAD cache becomes a recommendation: security-aware resolvers SHOULD implement one. The reason is operational experience that DNSSEC administrative errors can cause large increases in DNS traffic, and that such events are more likely and more damaging than first thought.
sections.eli5: Two helpers who used to be optional are now part of the official team. Also, a resolver should remember which answers were bad, so it does not keep asking the same broken question.

sections.title: Validation Rules That Protect Security
sections.content:
Four clarifications close gaps an attacker could use.

  • Nonexistence proofs. An NSEC or NSEC3 record from an ancestor delegation (NS bit set, SOA bit clear, signer shorter than the owner name) MUST NOT be used to prove that anything below the zone cut does not exist, apart from DS records. An NSEC or NSEC3 with the DNAME bit set MUST NOT prove that subdomains do not exist.
  • ANY queries. For QTYPE=*, every received RRset matching the QNAME and QCLASS MUST be validated, and if any fails, the answer is Bogus. A validator must not expect all records at the name.
  • CNAME check. For a NOERROR/NODATA response, validators MUST check the CNAME bit in the NSEC or NSEC3 type bitmap as well as the bit for the query type. Otherwise an attacker could strip a CNAME RRset and turn a positive answer into a NODATA answer.
  • Insecure delegations. To prove a delegation is not secure, a validator MUST check that the NS bit is present (or that the delegation is covered by an NSEC3 with the Opt-Out flag), in addition to the DS and SOA bits being absent. Otherwise a record for a non-delegation name could be reused to fake an unsigned delegation.
sections.eli5: These are the spots where a trickster could fool a checker. The checker now has to look at a few more things before trusting an answer that says nothing exists.

sections.title: Interoperability Rules for Validators and Signers
sections.content:
Section 5 of the RFC gathers twelve interoperability points. The main ones are:

  • Names inside NSEC RDATA are not lowercased for canonical form, while names inside RRSIG RDATA are. HINFO does not need case conversion, since it holds no domain names.
  • DS records using unknown or unsupported digest algorithms are treated like DS records for unsupported key algorithms. If none are left, the zone is treated as unsigned. For private algorithms, the resolver MUST fetch and examine the DNSKEY to see which algorithm is really in use.
  • A resolver SHOULD accept any valid RRSIG as sufficient and call an RRset Bogus only if all RRSIGs fail. This keeps techniques such as double-signature key rollover working.
  • The Key Tag for algorithm 1 uses the third-to-last and second-to-last octets of the public key modulus, not the fourth-to-last and third-to-last.
  • Resolvers MUST ignore the DO bit in responses. A query with the AD bit set now signals interest in the AD bit in the answer, and validating resolvers SHOULD set AD in a response only if the request had the DO or AD bit set.
  • Validating resolvers SHOULD set the CD bit on every upstream query.

For nested trust anchors the suggested default is the Accept Any Success policy: try all applicable anchors, and the result is Secure if any succeeds. Validators MUST disregard RRSIGs whose key or algorithm is absent from the DNSKEY RRset, since good rollover practice may require such signatures.
sections.eli5: Different programs read the same rules a little differently. This part says which reading to use so they all agree, and fixes one spot where the instructions had a typo.

sections.title: Mandatory Algorithm Rules and Key Use
sections.content:
The rule on which algorithms a zone must be signed with is restated more clearly. The presence of an algorithm in a zone's DS or DNSKEY RRset signals that it signs the whole zone. A signed zone MUST include a DNSKEY for each algorithm in its DS RRset and expected trust anchors, and MUST be signed with each algorithm in its DNSKEY RRset, though not with each key. Adding algorithms to the DNSKEY RRset that are not in the DS is allowed, but not the reverse.

This applies to servers, not validators. Validators SHOULD accept any single valid path, SHOULD NOT insist that all algorithms in the DS RRset work, and MUST NOT insist that all algorithms in the DNSKEY RRset work.

Different DNSKEYs may sign different parts of a zone, but nothing tells resolvers what a given key is for. Any DNSKEY in the signed DNSKEY RRset may authenticate any RRset, so a weaker key used for one purpose can sign anything. The SEP bit has no effect on how a key may be used.
sections.eli5: A zone must show every kind of signature it promises. A checker only needs one good signature to be satisfied, and a key labeled for one job can still be used for any job.

sections.title: Minor Corrections and the CD Bit Discussion
sections.content:
Small fixes include a pointer on finding the servers for a parent zone when sending DS queries, corrections to example names in RFC 4035 (for instance x.w.example.com should be x.w.example, and a.z.w.w.example should be a.z.w.example), and a fix to RFC 5155. There, the Type Bit Maps field regular expression should end in an asterisk rather than a plus sign, so an NSEC3 for an empty non-terminal can have an empty type bit map.

Appendix B explains why validators should always set the CD bit upstream. It compares three models: always set, never set when receiving CD=0, and sometimes set. Only the first is recommended; the other two are NOT RECOMMENDED. It also notes that a cached server failure (RCODE 2) may hide a validation failure, so a new query with CD set is needed in that case. Appendix C compares trust anchor policies: Closest Encloser, Accept Any Success, and preference based on source.
sections.eli5: The back pages fix typos in the examples and explain why one setting is better, with notes comparing different ways to choose which key to trust.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document adds SHA-2 and NSEC3 to the core protocol, and security considerations for those are in the documents that define them. The validation clarifications in Section 4 of the RFC are described as critical to preserving DNSSEC's security properties. Ignoring the interoperability points could limit the ability to change or expand DNSSEC later, for example by adding new algorithms.

The recommendation to always set the CD bit has a trade-off: the resolver will not benefit from stricter validation rules or a more complete set of trust anchors at an upstream validator.
sections.eli5: The fixes keep the lock honest. The one trade-off is that a resolver which always asks for unchecked answers cannot rely on a more careful checker upstream.

items.title: Ancestor delegation
items.text: NSEC or NSEC3 at a zone cut cannot prove nonexistence below the cut.

items.title: ANY query
items.text: Validate every received RRset; any failure makes the answer Bogus.

items.title: CNAME bit
items.text: NODATA proofs must also check the CNAME bit.

items.title: Insecure delegation
items.text: Require the NS bit, or an Opt-Out NSEC3 cover.
